title: Four genes that wound a skin cell back to the beginning

study.citation: Takahashi, K. & Yamanaka, S. (2006), "Induction of Pluripotent Stem Cells from Mouse Embryonic and Adult Fibroblast Cultures by Defined Factors", Cell 126(4), 663-676

tldr: Two scientists in Kyoto showed that just four genes can wind an adult skin cell all the way back to an embryo-like state able to become almost any tissue, resetting a cell's fate and reshaping regenerative medicine.

sections.body: Nearly every cell in your body carries the same DNA, yet a skin cell stays a skin cell and a nerve cell stays a nerve cell for life. Early in development, embryonic cells can still become any tissue at all. As cells take on a job, they seem to lock into that role for good. Biologists wondered whether the lock was truly permanent. Could you take a fully grown, specialized cell and wind it all the way back to the flexible, do-anything state of an embryo? A way to do that might sidestep the ethical and practical problems of taking stem cells from embryos.

Kazutoshi Takahashi and Shinya Yamanaka, working in Kyoto, guessed that a small set of master genes keeps embryonic cells flexible. They drew up a list of twenty-four candidate genes that are active in mouse embryonic stem cells. Using a harmless virus as a delivery truck, they inserted all twenty-four into ordinary skin cells, called fibroblasts, and watched for any that turned into stem-cell-like colonies. Some did. Then they removed the genes one at a time to see which ones the effect could not do without. The list collapsed to just four: Oct3/4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc.

Those four genes together reprogrammed adult skin cells into cells that behaved much like embryonic stem cells. The team named them induced pluripotent stem cells, or iPS cells, where "pluripotent" means able to become many different tissue types. The reprogrammed cells multiplied the same way, switched on the same signature genes, and, when injected into a developing mouse embryo, went on to help build many kinds of tissue throughout the animal. A grown-up cell had been wound back to a flexible early state using nothing more than a short recipe of four genes.

The result overturned the belief that specialization was a one-way street. It meant a patient's own skin cells could, in principle, be turned into stem cells and then coaxed into heart, nerve, or liver cells for repair, with no embryos involved and no immune rejection from foreign tissue. Labs now grow iPS cells to model diseases in a dish, test drugs on human cells, and pursue transplant therapies. Yamanaka shared the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, together with John Gurdon, for showing that a mature cell's fate can be reset.

The first iPS cells were a rough proof of the idea. Only a tiny fraction of the treated cells reprogrammed, and those early ones were an imperfect match for true embryonic stem cells. The method carried real risks. The delivery virus splices genes into the cell's own DNA, and one of the four factors, c-Myc, can help drive cancer. These were mouse cells; human iPS cells followed a year later, in 2007. Turning reprogrammed cells reliably and safely into specific tissues for real patients remains slow, painstaking work.

terms.def: Able to turn into many different cell types of the body, the way an early embryonic cell can.
A common cell found in skin and connective tissue; the ordinary grown-up cell the team started from.
Winding a specialized cell back to a younger, more flexible state instead of leaving it locked in one job.

takeaways: Specialization can be reversed: four genes can wind an adult skin cell back to an embryo-like, do-anything state.
These induced pluripotent stem cells avoid embryos, so a patient's own cells could one day be reprogrammed and grown into tissue for repair.
A messy first result can still be a landmark: the original iPS cells were inefficient and imperfect, yet they proved a cell's fate can be reset.

quiz.q: What did Takahashi and Yamanaka show was possible?
choices: Growing a whole mouse from a single skin cell
Reprogramming an adult specialized cell back into a flexible, embryo-like stem cell
Cloning an animal by transferring a nucleus
quiz.why: Their four factors turned ordinary adult fibroblasts into induced pluripotent stem cells that behaved like embryonic stem cells, showing specialization can be reversed. Nuclear-transfer cloning is a separate technique, and the study neither grew a whole animal from one skin cell nor cured cancer.

quiz.q: How did the team arrive at their four genes?
choices: They guessed the four at random
They used only a single gene from the start
They began with twenty-four candidate genes and removed them one at a time to find the essential ones
They copied the recipe from an earlier human study
quiz.why: They introduced all twenty-four pluripotency-associated genes together, saw reprogramming occur, then subtracted genes one by one until only the four indispensable ones remained: Oct3/4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc.

quiz.q: What is one honest limitation of the original 2006 experiment?
choices: It only worked on plant cells
The reprogrammed cells could never divide
It required a fresh embryo as its starting material
The reprogramming was very inefficient and used a virus plus a cancer-linked gene, all in mouse cells
quiz.why: Only a tiny fraction of cells reprogrammed, the delivery virus splices into the cell's DNA, the factor c-Myc can drive cancer, and the work was done in mice, with human iPS cells arriving in 2007. Avoiding embryos was actually a benefit of the method.
